doc.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Negotiating with each piano
summary: Peterson explains he must make a pact with each instrument in the first bars rather than fight it; Williams recalls Lester Young swapping horns.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well I’ve always had an intensity about playing piano. It’s a very special experience to me. Anytime that I sit down, I was telling Benny Green, who I love, a gifted pianist as you know, and I was telling him that every time I sit down with an instrument, I try to negotiate with that instrument. He was asking me how do you handle these different pianos? Some good, some not so good, some bad, thank God we don’t have too many bad ones nowadays. But I told him I says, the only way to overcome that is you have to sit down and negotiate with the instrument within the first few bars.
You make a pact with the instrument that you’re going to play it a certain way, and you’re going to talk to it a certain way. And hopefully it will respond to you.
There you go. That response is the thing, isn’t it?
That’s what it’s all about, isn’t it.
Oh, man, I never thought of it like that — negotiate.
Well, you can’t go in and fight it. You know, if you fight it you’re dead.
But you know that, you’ve seen it happen a lot of times.

Yes. Going in and fighting a piano. I don’t think so. Or any other instrument, really. I mean I think you have to negotiate, I mean I remember seeing Prez [Lester Young] take out a horn and say, “I’m going to have to put this girl away today, she’s not ready to play.” And put it away and took out another one, you know? Fun, really. But another thing that you did — when you branched out and started to do things with big orchestras, and I remember I think Ernie Wilkins did some of the work.
